note.explanation: A force is a vector, so it has both magnitude and direction. To add forces graphically, draw them head-to-tail. The resultant goes from the tail of the first force to the head of the last force.
examples: Forces of 4 N and 3 N placed at right angles have a resultant of 5 N.
In Example 4.1, the measured resultant is 7.1 cm. With the scale 100 N = 1 cm, its magnitude is 710 N.
note.simple: Put each force arrowhead-to-tail. The resultant is one arrow from where you started to where you finish.
note.checkQuestion: In Example 4.1, what force does a measured resultant length of 7.1 cm represent at the scale 100 N = 1 cm?
note.title: Adding forces by the head-to-tail rule
steps: Choose a suitable scale, such as 100 N = 1 cm.
Draw each force as an arrow using the scale and the given direction.
Place the tail of each new arrow at the head of the previous arrow.
Draw the resultant from the tail of the first arrow to the head of the last arrow.
Measure the resultant and use the scale to find its magnitude; read its direction from the diagram.
note.answer: The resultant is the single force that has the same effect as the forces acting together.

written.text: What are rectangular components of a vector and their values?
written.finalAnswer: The rectangular components are the components along perpendicular x- and y-axes: F_x = F cosθ and F_y = F sinθ, where θ is measured from the x-axis.

explain.title: Forces are vectors
explain.body: Your textbook says: “As forces are vectors, so forces can also be added by head-to-tail rule.” A force has a magnitude and a direction, so both must be shown when you draw it.

explain.title: Use the head-to-tail rule
explain.body: Draw the first force, then start the next force at its arrowhead. Keep joining the forces in this way. Draw the resultant from the starting tail to the final arrowhead.

explain.title: Use the scale to find the answer
explain.body: Choose a scale, draw the forces, and measure the resultant. Convert its measured length back to newtons using the same scale. Its direction is the angle it makes with the chosen axis.

explain.title: Changing the order does not change the resultant
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Remember that the resultant is the same for any order of addition of vectors.” The drawn path may look different when the order changes, but the resultant has the same magnitude and direction.

mistakes: Drawing all the force tails from the same point instead of arranging them head-to-tail.
Forgetting to convert a force magnitude into a length using the selected scale.
Drawing the resultant from the wrong ends; it must start at the first tail and end at the last head.
Giving the resultant magnitude but leaving out its direction.
Using a scale to convert the resultant length incorrectly or not stating the scale.
